title: Measuring build time vs. solve time

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A nightly MILP run takes 50 s: 1 s to load data, 3 s to build the model, and 46 s that the solver reports as its solve_time. A colleague makes the builder ten times faster and nothing else changes. About how long does the run take now?

options.text: About 5 s, because the whole run becomes ten times faster
options.says: Only the build got faster. The solve, 46 of the 50 s, is untouched; the lesson's medium run spent 94% of its time solving.

options.text: About 47 s, because only the 3 s of building becomes shorter
options.says: Right: the build drops from 3 s to 0.3 s and the other 47 s stay, so the run saves under 3 s.

options.text: About 25 s, because a faster build also halves the solver's work
options.says: A faster builder makes the same model, so the solver has the same work. The lesson's builders export identical models.

options.text: About 50 s, because build time never changes a MILP run at all
options.says: Saving 2.7 s is small here but real; on GridCap large the build was 15% of the run, and twice the LP relaxation's solve.

origin.section: A Run Has Phases, and Each Phase Gets Its Own Clock

questions.stem: The old builder was timed once on Monday at 0.80 s. The new builder was timed once on Tuesday at 0.40 s, on the same server. What does this support?

options.text: The new builder is twice as fast, since the server was the same both days
options.says: The same build measured 0.021 s and 0.037 s in two runs a minute apart on one machine; a day apart, the difference could be the machine.

options.text: The new builder is slower, since a single first run is always the fastest one
options.says: The other way round: the cold first build was the slowest sample in both of the lesson's runs.

options.text: The new builder is twice as fast, since one run each is all a ratio needs
options.says: One sample per builder carries all of the machine's noise into the ratio; the lesson repeats and takes medians.

options.text: Little yet, since neither was warmed up, repeated or timed side by side
options.says: Right: warm both up, repeat in one process, and compare ratios taken round by round.

origin.section: One Timing Is an Anecdote: Warm Up, Repeat, and Report the Median and Range

questions.stem: Median build times are 0.5 s for 2,500 projects, 2 s for 5,000 and 8 s for 10,000. If the trend holds, about how long will 20,000 projects take?

options.text: About 32 s, since every doubling has multiplied the time by four
options.says: Right: the growth exponent is 2 (log 4 / log 2), so the next doubling multiplies 8 s by 4 again.

options.text: About 16 s, since doubling the projects always doubles the time
options.says: That holds for an exponent of 1, a linear builder; these times quadruple at each doubling.

options.text: About 14 s, since each doubling has added the same six seconds
options.says: The added time is not fixed: it went from 1.5 s to 6 s. Growth is read as a ratio, the slope of log time against log size.

options.text: About 8 s, since build time stops growing once a model is large
options.says: Nothing in the measurements levels off; the slow builder's compared rows grew fourfold at every doubling up to 10,000.

origin.section: Time at Several Sizes to Learn How Build Time Grows
